events.title: Telegram
events.text:
During last night's large-scale Russian missile attack on Ukraine, the interception rate of Kh-101 cruise missiles was unusually low - one of the lowest so far this year. 
Out of roughly 48 Kh-101 cruise missiles launched, I could only confirm around 10 interceptions, mainly by fighter jets. 
In my opinion, this was caused by Ukraine's ongoing F-16 maintenance crisis, and due to the fact that Russia is striking areas of Ukraine closer to the border, providing Ukrainian air defences with much less time to shoot down the missiles. The missiles also flew in very large groups immediately towards their targets, without changing course much, completely overwhelming Ukrainian air defences. 
The Kh-101s impacted three cities - Kremenchuk (Poltava Oblast), Pryluky (Chernihiv Oblast), and Oleksandriya (Kirovohrad Oblast).
Most of the impacts occurred in Kremenchuk, while around a dozen occurred in Oleksandriya, along with another dozen or so in Pryluky. Multiple different locations in Kremenchuk, including the hydroelectric power plant, were hit. 
The interception rate on Kalibrs was much higher (roughly 9 out of 12 missiles were shot down), with the remaining 3 striking two different targets in Kremenchuk.
As for ballistics, patriot systems in Kyiv shot down ~4 out of 10 Iskander-M/RM-48U S-400 missiles, and air defences near the city of Ukrainka in Kyiv Oblast shot down both Oniks-M supersonic cruise missiles targeting the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant. The 2 Zircons both impacted Trypillya TPP.

events.text:
🔍 Turkish military buildup in Saudi Arabia may initially be limited to special forces and air defenses – reports
Turkey is planning to deploy additional equipment, technicians, emergency response teams, and support personnel to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Pact, Turkish officials told Middle East Eye, commenting on [the October 5 joint statement](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75697) issued by the pact’s signatories.
Turkey has maintained technical teams, air defense systems, and electronic warfare equipment in the Gulf kingdom since 2025 to protect critical infrastructure, including energy facilities.
One official said that limited forces are being deployed under a 2010 military training agreement between Saudi Arabia and Turkey, but any major deployment would require parliamentary approval. The official also noted that the Mecca Pact has yet to be ratified by Turkey’s Grand National Assembly.
The Turkish parliament could formally authorize the deployment of a limited number of Turkish special forces as early as later this month, according to another official.
Separate sources told MEE that Turkey could also send an undisclosed number of pilots and aircraft to Saudi Arabia to counter Houthi-launched drones and ballistic missiles.
According to Saudi sources cited by the publication, Turkish troops would operate alongside Saudi and Pakistani forces from a joint coordination center, while Turkey’s command unit would operate from a separate facility.
The primary purpose of the military presence is reportedly to protect critical Saudi infrastructure, particularly the East-West Oil Pipeline, Tasnim News reports.
